L2@P0: Towards Quantum-Safe Smart
L3@P0: Contracts on Hyperledger Fabric
L4@P0: Author: Jaylan Lee (6104223)
L5@P0: thesis advisor: Georgios Smaragdakis

L11@P1-2: iiAbstract
L12@P2: Blockchain technology has had a big impact on digital transactions and data
L13@P2: management, providing a decentralized, transparent, and immutable ledger.
L14@P2: Private blockchains, unlike public blockchains, are restricted to a pre-selected
L15@P2: group of participants, making them more suitable for controlled environments
L16@P2: such as enterprises, governments, or academic institutions. Hyperledger Fabric
L17@P2: (HLF) is a widely used framework for private blockchain technology, designed
L18@P2: for enterprise use.
L19@P2: With quantum computers on the rise, commonly used cryptographic algorithms
L20@P2: are increasingly at risk of becoming obsolete. Blockchain networks rely extensively on these primitives. This reliance makes them particularly vulnerable
L21@P2: to advances in quantum computing. In order to counter this vulnerability,
L22@P2: post-quantum algorithms have seen rising popularity in the cryptographic community.
L23@P2: This thesis focuses on securing private blockchains built on HLF against potential quantum adversaries using post-quantum cryptographic primitives. We
L24@P2: implement ML-DSA, Vesper, and TDUE as smart contracts for digital signing,
L25@P2: zero-knowledge proofs, and updatable encryption, respectively, and report on
L26@P2: their performance. Furthermore, we build on top of Fabric Private Chaincode
L27@P2: to keep the contract application state confidential. While overall performance is
L28@P2-3: not yet competitive with classical cryptographic primitives, we show that postquantum primitives have promising potential for use in private blockchains.Acknowledgements

L162@P8: Introduction
L163@P8: With quantum computers on the rise, cryptographic algorithms that are currently deemed
L164@P8: as the standard are increasingly at risk of becoming obsolete. Current algorithms such
L165@P8: as RSA, ECC, and ECDSA could be cryptanalytically broken with a sufficiently powerful
L166@P8: quantum computer using Shor’s algorithm (7, 8). While quantum computing is still in its
L167@P8: early stages, its eventual advancement will pose a vulnerability risk on classical cryptographic primitives. Even without an immediate quantum threat, "harvest now, decrypt
L168@P8: later" programs still pose a risk on the long-term security of encrypted storage and communication. Data that is sensitive today, may remain sensitive in the future.
L169@P8: To expand on this topic, blockchain networks make extensive use of cryptographic primitives and rely almost exclusively on the hardness of currently used algorithms for their
L170@P8: security. This reliance makes them particularly vulnerable to advances in quantum computing. Generally, blockchain networks use cryptographic primitives such as encryption
L171@P8: and digital signing algorithms to manage identities, execute and endorse transactions, distribute new blocks, query the ledger, etc. Blockchain technology has seen widespread
L172@P8: applications due to the qualities of its architecture, which inherently grant immutability,
L173@P8: decentralisation, and transparency. The emergence of quantum computing poses a threat
L174@P8: to these qualities.
L175@P8: In order to counter the vulnerability posed by these algorithms, a new suite of postquantum algorithms (also referred to as quantum-resistant algorithms) has seen rising
L176@P8: popularity in the cryptographic community. These algorithms are currently thought to
L177@P8: remain secure against cryptanalytic attacks, even under the assumption of the existence of
L178@P8: quantum computers. One approach to post-quantum algorithms can be reduced to latticebased cryptography, with hard problems such as LWE (9) and SIS (10). In 2024, NIST
L179@P8: has released three final versions of the first post-quantum cryptographic standards, two of
L180@P8: which utilise lattice-based cryptography (11).
L181@P8: This thesis focuses on securing private blockchains. Unlike public blockchains, private
L182@P8: blockchains are restricted to a pre-selected group of participants, making them more suitable for controlled environments such as enterprises, governments, or academic institutions.
L183@P8: A widely used framework for private blockchain technology is Hyperledger Fabric, which
L184@P8: is an open-source permissioned blockchain platform designed for enterprise use. We aim
L185@P8: to secure private blockchains, particularly those built on Hyperledger Fabric, against the
L186@P8: potential threat of quantum computers.
L187@P8: To illustrate the practical relevance of cryptography on blockchains, consider the following scenario:
L188@P8-9: 11. INTRODUCTION
L189@P9: Motivating Example: Blockchain Library with Subscription Payments
L190@P9: Consider a blockchain-based library system called Rainforest, where users can borrow books by making monthly subscription payments. Rainforest uses a private
L191@P9: blockchain to host their books and manage payments.
L192@P9: Books are stored as encrypted files on the ledger, all under the same key, and users
L193@P9: get the decryption keys upon successful payment. Every month, the keys get updated
L194@P9: to ensure that users can only access the books they have paid for in the current month.
L195@P9: Suppose a user named Alice wants to apply for a subscription. She needs to prove
L196@P9: that she has sufficient funds to make the payment without revealing her account balance or transaction history. To do this, Alice uses a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate that she owns at least the required amount of funds. This proof is verified by
L197@P9: the Rainforest blockchain network, allowing Alice to proceed with the payment without exposing her (sensitive) financial details. The payment request is signed by her
L198@P9: private key, preventing unauthorized financial transactions.
L199@P9: This example illustrates how a private blockchain can be used to manage sensitive data,
L200@P9: such as financial transactions and personal information, while maintaining user privacy.
L201@P9: The use of zero-knowledge proofs allows users to prove their eligibility for actions (like payments) without revealing sensitive information, while digital signatures ensure the integrity
L202@P9: and authenticity of transactions. At its core, the Rainforest library relies on updatable encryption to manage access to the books.
L203@P9: Building on this motivating example, we now formalize the research question addressed
L204@P9: in this thesis:
L205@P9: RQ. How can post-quantum cryptographic modules be integrated into Hyperledger Fabric
L206@P9: while preserving confidentiality, and how do they perform in practice?
L207@P9: Contributions. We propose replacements for three cryptographic primitives, including
L208@P9: the digital signing algorithm present in the architecture of Hyperledger Fabric. We implement ML-DSA (signing algorithm), Vesper (zero-knowledge proof), and TDUE (updatable
L209@P9: encryption) as smart contracts on top of the existing architecture, and report on their performance to demonstrate their feasibility for use in practical scenarios. The novel aspect
L210@P9: of this research lies in the practical integration of multiple post-quantum cryptographic
L211@P9: primitives into a real-world private blockchain framework, while using trusted computing
L212@P9: technology to hide the application state.
L213@P9: 1.1 Organization
L214@P9: First, we cover related work in Section 2. In Chapter 3, we provide the necessary background on the cryptographic primitives used in this thesis. Chapters 4, 5, and 6 present
L215@P9: a brief overview of the three cryptographic primitives we implement, namely ML-DSA,
L216@P9: TDUE, and Vesper, respectively. Chapter 7 covers the architecture of blockchain systems,
L217@P9: with a focus on Hyperledger Fabric. In Chapter 8, we present a high-level overview of
L218@P9: our design for three modules that implement the cryptographic primitives in Hyperledger
L219@P9-10: 21.1 Organization
L220@P10: Fabric. In Chapter 9, we describe the implementation details of these modules. We benchmark the performance of our implementations in Chapter 10, and discuss the results in
L221@P10: Chapter 11. Finally, we conclude our work in Chapter 12.
L222@P10-11: 32
L223@P11: Related Work
L224@P11: In this chapter, we discuss related (scientific) works that share similar goals and/or methodology to ours.
L225@P11: Post-quantum distributed ledger technology: a systematic survey. Parida et al.
L226@P11: (2023) (12) investigate the status quo of post-quantum cryptosystems within the framework
L227@P11: of (public) blockchains. The article classifies approaches aimed at fortifying blockchains
L228@P11: with post-quantum cryptography. The article also identifies specific (quantum) weaknesses
L229@P11: in current blockchain systems, such as speeding up hash collision using Grover’s algorithm
L230@P11: (13) and breaking classical encryption using Shor’s algorithm (7). The article does not
L231@P11: focus on private blockchains, such as Hyperledger Fabric, and does not provide a concrete
L232@P11: architectural design for integrating post-quantum cryptography into such systems.
L233@P11: Algorand. A practical example of post-quantum distributed ledger technology (PQDLT)
L234@P11: is Algorand (14), first proposed in a whitepaper in 2017. In 2022, Algorand announced its
L235@P11: transition to a post-quantum secure blockchain. They started this endeavour by replacing
L236@P11: elliptic curve signing with FALCON (15), a post-quantum signature scheme based on lattice
L237@P11: trapdoors. The consensus mechanism of Algorand still relies on the quantum-vulnerable
L238@P11: Verifiable Randomness Function (VRF) (16), but there are plans to replace it with a postquantum secure VRF in the future.
L239@P11: PQFabric: A Permissioned Blockchain Secure from Both Classical and Quantum Attacks. There have been multiple previous attempts at replacing classical primitives within Hyperledger Fabric with post-quantum primitives. These efforts have mostly
L240@P11: focused on replacing ECDSA with either hybrid schemes (17, 18, 19) or non-standardized
L241@P11: post-quantum algorithms (20). Since the NIST standardized post-quantum algorithms in
L242@P11: 2024 were released, there have been works that have started to replace ECDSA with the
L243@P11: standardized ML-DSA (21). What separates our thesis from these works, is that we focus on providing a more complete post-quantum platform for HLF by not only replacing
L244@P11: the crucial elements, but also providing two additional cryptographic primitives. Combined with our efforts to keep the application state confidential by using FPC, our work
L245@P11: can be viewed as more of a foundational set to develop complete applications for private
L246@P11: blockchains.
